paragraphs: Friend, here's what I love about Agur. He opens by saying he's weary and ignorant, and then he asks some of the biggest questions in the whole Bible: "Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands?" (Proverbs 30:1-4). Real wisdom starts when you admit you don't have it all figured out. The One who made the wind and the waters is the One worth trusting, and Agur says "Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him." (Proverbs 30:5).

So Agur doesn't ask God for a fancy life. He asks to keep falsehood far from him, and for "neither poverty nor riches," just "the bread that is my portion." (Proverbs 30:8). He knows too much could make him forget God, and too little could push him to steal (Proverbs 30:9). Then he gives us pictures of what life without that kind of wisdom looks like: people proud in their own eyes, hearts that always shout "Give!", and a person who wipes her mouth and says, "I have done nothing wrong." (Proverbs 30:12, 15, 20). Friend, that is a lot of us on a bad day, and I'm raising my hand first.

And the little guys? They get the spotlight. The ants, the rock badgers, the locusts and the lizard are small, yet Agur calls them "exceedingly wise." (Proverbs 30:24). You don't need to be the biggest or the loudest to live wisely. You need to be humble, trust God's words, and, as Agur says, put your hand over your mouth before pride and anger stir up strife (Proverbs 30:32-33).
